title: Non-Conservative Forces
short_intro: Non-conservative forces are interactions where the work done in moving a particle between two points depends on the specific path taken. In the presence of such forces, mechanical energy is not conserved and typically dissipates into thermal or internal energy.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Identification of conservative vs non-conservative forces, basic work-energy theorem application with friction, and simple numericals on work done by sliding friction.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Path dependence of line integrals, mathematical conditions for non-conservativity (curl F not equal to zero), velocity-dependent forces like viscous drag, and Lagrangian formulations with Rayleigh dissipation functions.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Path Dependence
bullets: A force F is non-conservative if the line integral of the force around any closed path is non-zero: ∮ F • dr ≠ 0.
The work done by a non-conservative force depends on the trajectory or path connecting the initial and final positions.
Examples include kinetic friction, viscous drag, and air resistance.

concept_notes.heading: Violation of Mechanical Energy Conservation
bullets: Total mechanical energy E = K + U is not conserved when non-conservative forces act on a system.
The work-energy theorem states that the total work done by all forces equals the change in kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK.
Writing W_net = W_c + W_nc, where W_c is conservative and W_nc is non-conservative work, leads to W_nc = ΔK + ΔU = ΔE.

concept_notes.heading: Velocity Dependence and Dissipation
bullets: Many non-conservative forces, such as fluid drag (F = -bv or F = -cv<sup>2</sup>), depend explicitly on the velocity of the particle.
These forces invariably oppose motion, continuously removing mechanical energy from the system and converting it into heat or sound.
Because they depend on velocity, they cannot be derived from a scalar potential energy function U(r).

concept_notes.heading: Mathematical Test for Conservativity
bullets: For a force field to be conservative, its curl must vanish identically throughout the region: ∇ × F = 0.
If ∇ × F ≠ 0, the force field possesses circulation and is strictly non-conservative.
Forces like the magnetic Lorentz force or frictional forces fail the curl test or are velocity-dependent in ways that preclude a scalar potential.

derivations.title: Work Done by Sliding Friction along Different Paths
derivations.conditions: A block of mass m is moved on a horizontal rough surface with coefficient of kinetic friction μ_k.
steps: Consider moving a block from point A(0,0) to B(L,0) along a straight path directly along the x-axis. The normal force is N = mg, and the frictional force is f_k = μ_k mg pointing opposite to displacement. The work done is W_1 = ∫ (-μ_k mg) dx from x = 0 to L, yielding W_1 = -μ_k mg L.

Now consider moving the same block along a semicircular path of radius R from A(0,0) to B(πR,0) in the xy-plane, where πR = L. At every infinitesimal displacement ds, the frictional force opposes the tangential motion: f_k • ds = -f_k ds.
Integrating the friction force along the arc length yields W_2 = - ∫ μ_k mg ds = -μ_k mg ∫ ds = -μ_k mg (πR). Since πR > L, |W_2| > |W_1|, demonstrating path dependence.
derivations.result: W_friction = -μ_k mg S, where S is the total actual path length traversed.

derivations.title: Work-Energy Theorem with Non-Conservative Forces
derivations.conditions: A particle moves under the combined action of conservative internal forces and external non-conservative forces.
steps: Start with Newton's second law: F_net = F_c + F_nc = m (dv/dt), where F_c is conservative and F_nc is non-conservative.
Take the dot product of the equation with displacement differential dr = v dt and integrate from initial position 1 to final position 2: ∫ (F_c • dr) + ∫ (F_nc • dr) = ∫ m (dv/dt) • v dt.
Recognize that the work done by conservative forces is related to potential energy change: ∫ F_c • dr = -Delta U, and the right-hand side integrates to kinetic energy change ΔK.
Rearrange the terms to express the non-conservative work: W_nc = ΔK - (-Delta U) = ΔK + ΔU = ΔE.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Work vs Path Length for Friction
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A linear graph plotting Work Magnitude (|W|) on the y-axis against Path Length (s) on the x-axis, showing a straight line passing through the origin with slope μ_k mg.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The work magnitude increases linearly with the distance traversed, highlighting that longer paths suffer greater energy dissipation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in conceptual MCQs asking why friction cannot have a potential energy function.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mechanical Energy Decay with Time
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An exponential decay curve plotting Total Mechanical Energy E(t) on the y-axis against time t on the x-axis for an oscillator under damping.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Energy is monotonically lost due to non-conservative damping forces until the system reaches rest.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to interpret damped harmonic oscillation questions in PGT mechanics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Joule's Paddle Wheel Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup showing falling weights connected via pulleys to a paddle wheel immersed in an insulated container of water, with a thermometer.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the mechanical equivalent of heat by showing that work done by non-conservative gravitational/tension forces converted via friction/viscosity raises water temperature.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Theoretical linkage between mechanical work done by non-conservative forces and internal thermal energy generation.

solved_numericals.question: A block of mass 2 kg is pulled across a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force over a distance of 5 m. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the floor is 0.3. Find the work done by the frictional force. (Take g = 10 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Identify the given values: mass m = 2 kg, distance s = 5 m, coefficient of kinetic friction \mu_k = 0.3, g = 10 m/s^2.
Calculate the normal force N = mg = 2 \times 10 = 20 N.
Calculate the magnitude of kinetic friction f_k = \mu_k N = 0.3 \times 20 = 6 N.
Calculate the work done by friction: W_f = -f_k s = -6 \times 5 = -30 J.

solved_numericals.question: A particle of mass 1 kg moves in a horizontal xy-plane under a non-conservative force given by F = (-y i + x j) N. Calculate the work done by this force along a quarter circle of radius R = 2 m from (2, 0) to (0, 2).
solution_steps: Express the position vector and its differential along the circular path: x = R cos(\theta), y = R sin(\theta), where R = 2.
The displacement differential is dr = dx i + dy j. In polar coordinates or parametric form: dx = -R sin(\theta) d\theta and dy = R cos(\theta) d\theta.
Substitute into the force vector: F = (-R sin(\theta) i + R cos(\theta) j).
Compute the dot product F • dr = (-R sin(\theta))(-R sin(\theta) d\theta) + (R cos(\theta))(R cos(\theta) d\theta) = R^2 (sin^2(\theta) + cos^2(\theta)) d\theta = R^2 d\theta.
Integrate from \theta = 0 to \theta = \pi/2: W = \int_0^{\pi/2} R^2 d\theta = R^2 [\theta]_0^{\pi/2} = (2^2)(\pi/2) = 4(\pi/2) = 2\pi J.

solved_numericals.question: A small body of mass 0.5 kg falls from rest through a viscous medium that exerts a drag force F_d = -bv, where b = 2 Ns/m. Find its velocity as a function of time t. (Take g = 9.8 m/s^2)
solution_steps: Set up Newton's second law along the vertical downward direction (y-axis): mg - bv = m (dv/dt).
Rearrange into a standard linear first-order differential equation: dv/dt + (b/m)v = g.
Substitute the values: b/m = 2 / 0.5 = 4 s^{-1}, and g = 9.8 m/s^2. Thus, dv/dt + 4v = 9.8.
Multiply by integrating factor e^{\int 4 dt} = e^{4t}: d(v e^{4t})/dt = 9.8 e^{4t}.
Integrate both sides using the initial condition v(0) = 0: v(t) = (9.8 / 4) (1 - e^{-4t}) = 2.45 (1 - e^{-4t}) m/s.

assumptions_and_limitations: Macroscopic friction is assumed to obey Amontons-Coulomb laws where the kinetic friction coefficient is independent of sliding speed and apparent contact area, which breaks down at extremely high velocities or nanocontacts.
Viscous drag formulations assume specific flow regimes (such as linear Stokes drag or quadratic Newton drag) and fail when turbulence or compressibility effects become prominent.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Friction always does negative work, so total energy of the universe decreases.
common_misconceptions.correct: Friction does negative mechanical work, converting mechanical energy into thermal energy; total energy remains conserved.
common_misconceptions.why: Energy is conserved overall; non-conservative forces only transfer mechanical energy into internal thermal energy modes.

common_misconceptions.wrong: If the work done by a force between two points is zero, the force must be conservative.
common_misconceptions.correct: Zero work along one specific path does not guarantee zero work along all paths or zero work around a closed loop.
common_misconceptions.why: Conservativity requires zero work for *every* arbitrary closed path, not merely a specific round trip.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Non-conservative forces cannot be expressed as analytical functions of position or velocity.
common_misconceptions.correct: Forces like F = -bv or position-dependent non-conservative circulating forces are fully expressed via analytical vector functions.
common_misconceptions.why: An analytical formula can define a non-conservative vector field perfectly; the distinguishing feature is the non-zero curl or path dependence.

quick_revision: Non-conservative forces exhibit path-dependent work and non-zero closed-loop line integrals: ∮ F • dr ≠ 0.
The presence of non-conservative forces implies that mechanical energy changes by exactly the work they perform: W_nc = ΔE.
Non-Conservative Work Line Integral: W_{nc} = \oint \mathbf{F}_{nc} \cdot d\mathbf{r} \neq 0
